items.title: Ever Inherited a System With Unclear Reasoning Behind Its Design, Making Any Change Feel Risky?
items.summary:
Ever opened a legacy system and thought: “Why is it built like this?”

No documentation. No clear tradeoffs. No one remembers the original reasoning. And suddenly every “small change” feels like defusing a bomb.

In this short, Matt Erman, author of Grokking Software Architecture, explains how to approach inherited systems when the architecture decisions aren’t obvious — and how to make changes with more confidence instead of fear.

Because the scariest code isn’t always the messiest code. It’s the code where nobody knows why it works.

Learn more: https://hubs.la/Q04gYZN10

#SoftwareArchitecture #SystemDesign #LegacyCode #SoftwareEngineering #TechnicalDebt #TechLeadership #Programming #Coding #ManningBooks

items.title: AMA with Luis Serrano
items.summary:
Luis Serrano is an AI scientist and educator. Previously, he was a Machine Learning Engineer at Google and Lead Artificial Intelligence Educator at Apple.

In this session, we’ll ask these questions:
- Why does ML feel so intimidating to beginners?
- Who is Grokking Algorithms book really for?
- What is new in the latest edition of the book?
- Why do ML fundamentals still matter in the age of LLMs?
- Where should someone start with machine learning today?
- How can learners move beyond just copying tutorials?
- Why is visual intuition so important in ML?
- How do you explain overfitting in simple terms?
- How should beginners choose the right ML algorithm?
- Why is accuracy sometimes a bad metric?
- How much math do people really need for ML?
- How does the book make ML practical with Python?
- Why do neural networks feel like magic?
- What’s the simplest way to understand neural networks?
- What should readers be able to do after finishing the book?

This is a live, interactive session, bring your questions for Luis.
 
We will also giveaway Ebooks to 2 lucky winners during the session. Comment #AI to enter the raffle!

items.title: Omnigent: Composition, Control, and Collaboration for AI Agents
items.summary:
Denny Lee is PM Director, Startups & Ecosystem at Databricks, a longtime Apache Spark, MLflow, and Delta Lake contributor — and one of the people behind Omnigent, the open-source meta-harness Databricks just released under Apache 2.0. He joins Demetrios to explain why the industry is moving from models to harnesses to meta-harnesses, why token spend is replaying the CapEx-to-OpEx shift all over again, and why he's using debating AI agents to plan a matcha farm in Taiwan.

In this episode:

🍵 Agents as research partners — Denny uses dueling agents to scout matcha-growing regions in Taiwan, down to soil pH, elevation, and processing infrastructure

🥊 Why agents should debate each other — letting two models argue surfaces the questions you didn't know to ask

🔱 Forking conversations — the missing UX pattern: branch a session, keep the shared context, explore two threads in parallel

🧠 The meta-harness layer — how Omnigent sits above Claude Code, Codex, Pi, and custom agents so models and harnesses become hot-swappable parts

👥 The two-pizza rule for agents — military span-of-control logic says you can manage 5–7 agents before you lose the thread

💸 Tokenomics is the new DevOps — the CapEx→OpEx playbook repeats: give developers spend visibility, keep central governance for the rest

🛡️ Policies, budgets, and guardrails — enforcing cost caps and approval rules at the harness layer instead of inside prompts

🤖 Auto model selection — why classic machine learning (not another LLM) may be the right way to route tasks to cheap vs. frontier models

✍️ "Created by" vs. "assisted by" — the open source accountability debate: whoever submits the code owns the code

🗄️ Databases are back — agents need cheap, stateful memory, which is why Postgres, Lakebase, and serverless databases are having a moment

If you're building with coding agents, managing AI spend, or trying to keep up with the harness arms race, this one's for you.

Links & Resources:

Omnigent (open source): https://www.databricks.com/blog/introducing-omnigent-meta-harness-combine-control-and-share-your-agents
Omnigent GitHub: https://github.com/databricks/omnigent

Denny's blog: https://dennyglee.com

items.title: This Data Scientist Used AI to Save His Dog
items.summary: In episode 1009 of the SuperDataScience Podcast, Jon Krohn talks with Steve Mock, Investor at Blumberg Capital about an incredible story from aisavedme.org where an Australian data scientist used AI to sequence his dog's cancer tumor and create a custom experimental treatment. This groundbreaking approach led to the dog's tumors shrinking, showcasing AI's profound impact on healthcare and personalized medicine.

Every lesson pairs a short video with an interactive notebook and quiz, plus an AI course assistant available to help when you get stuck. All you need is a free Wolfram U account.

Enroll at https://wolfr.am/Creative-Computation-MOOC and start building your creative computation portfolio.
